source_resolution.reason: The 1991 article body remained unavailable after the recorded initial attempt and five recovery retries: one metadata-only DOI response, one unauthorized text-mining response, a blocked request for a distinct 1988 version, and three DOI fetches returning an 11-character HTML error body. No full-text stamp is claimed. The article is dropped as evidentiary support. Its APX class statement is supplied as a local definition over the preceding finite-instance optimization model, and the selected APX-hardness/completeness convention and L-reduction transfer are supplied locally with declared dependencies. This makes no claim that L-reductions are the unique APX convention and makes no concrete target APX-hardness or completeness claim.
source_resolution.search_summary: Searched Google Scholar for the exact 1991 title and full-text copies, for APX-hard/L-reduction definitions, and for every-APX-problem L-reduction wording; checked OpenAlex repository-location metadata; and inspected the accessible author-hosted full text of a relevant approximation-classes article. No authoritative accessible text confirming a canonical APX/L-reduction convention was located. The accessible Crescenzi–Kann–Silvestri–Trevisan text explicitly cautions against treating L-reductions as a general completeness notion for computational classes such as APX, so it is not used to support the selected local convention.

alternatives.argument: Define APX locally as the class of finite-instance optimization problems from def-optimization-problem-and-approximation-ratio that admit one polynomial-time fixed-factor approximation in the stated objective direction. The prerequisite supplies polynomially bounded feasible encodings, polynomial feasibility/value operations, attained optima, and nonnegative values. This is an explicit definition rather than a claim attributed to the inaccessible article.

Using the local APX definition and the separately stated L-reduction, define the selected convention: every APX source must L-reduce to an APX-hard target, and completeness adds target membership. This is a stipulated convention, not an assertion that the literature has a unique APX-hardness reduction notion or that any target in this scope meets the definition.

The local proof derives the relative-error transfer from the two L-reduction inequalities for positive optimum, handles either zero optimum using nonnegative values and the ratio guarantee, and composes reductions by composing their instance/solution maps and multiplying constants: (a,b) then (a',b') gives (aa',bb'). Therefore APX-hardness under the selected convention transfers by composition. A no-PTAS gap result is not used as an APX-hardness proof.
